title: Number-sequence keys in direct and chain views
question: Do source-defined integer sequences produce unusually concentrated output under direct or chain-increment decoding of nine LP2 sections?
reader_question: Could prime, Fibonacci or totient numbers be the key?
summary: The full published source grid reproduces, but its selected coincidence peaks remain compatible with matched shuffled sections once section choice is included.
finding: All 135 printed source top-three candidates and nine solved-text running-key rows replay exactly. Both planted direct and chain prime-key streams pass the full-grid positive controls. The smallest LP2 section tail is 4/100 on pages 00–02; a simple nine-section choice bound is 36/100. This bounded coincidence scan supplies no recovered reading or supported key.
limitations: The source grid uses 24 named sequences, offsets 0–199, two signs, five views and whole-section coincidence as its score. Several names and views are exact duplicates or complements; they are retained as named source settings, not counted as distinct ideas. The 99-shuffle section controls preserve rune counts but do not model every possible cipher or an English reading. The prime-index stream is ineligible for the observed section lengths.
next_steps: A specific sequence proposal should freeze its source, phase, boundary and decoder, then predict a held-out readable result rather than selecting a high coincidence peak.

scope.representation: Nine pinned relikd unsolved sections, their generated Leo dataset indices, forward and reverse nonrepeat chain increments and original or Atbash GP29 runes.
scope.procedure: Replay the named 24-sequence, 200-offset, two-sign grid on five source streams; retain three best rows per section and stream. Replay the source solved-text running-key arm. For each section, select the grid maximum and compare with the same selection on 99 rune-order shuffles. Gate on planted raw and chain prime-key streams first.
scope.parameters: Source sequence rules from pinned tests4.py; GP29 and chain Z28/Z29; random.Random(330104/330105) planted controls and 330104 section shuffles; plus-one selected-grid tails.
scope.exclusions: Other key sources, offsets outside 0–199, alternative section joins or boundaries, English scoring, held-out plaintext and every cipher outside the declared source grid.

reproduction.command: python experiments/records/leo-chain-sequence-keys/run.py --source-root LEO --text-root RELIKD --check && python experiments/records/leo-chain-sequence-keys/check.py --source-root LEO --text-root RELIKD
reproduction.environment: Python 3.9+ with NumPy and Numba for the full grid; separate checker uses the standard library. LEO and RELIKD are pinned checkouts, with LEO dataset.json generated from RELIKD; source hashes are checked before computation.

sources.label: Pinned Leo source test and receipt

visuals.caption: Source-grid maxima compared with matched rune-order shuffles, by LP2 section.

reader_finding: Familiar number sequences yielded no established reading. The strongest rune-frequency pattern was also reached by 3 of 99 shuffled sections and did not clear the comparison after allowing for the nine sections searched.
reader_limit: This compared symbol frequencies, not readable sentences, using 24 named sequences, offsets 0–199 and five fixed ways of representing the runes. Other key sources, offsets and section boundaries remain open.
